analysis.one_liner: Gives interstate truck drivers the same right to overtime pay as most other workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: introduced in November 2023, it sat in committee with 3 cosponsors and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal wage law requires employers to pay time-and-a-half after 40 hours a week, but since 1938 truck drivers employed by motor carriers have been exempt from that rule. This bill would delete that exemption, so covered truckers would earn overtime like most other workers. It was sent to a House committee and was never considered before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Truck drivers employed by motor carriers — long-haul and other over-the-road drivers who routinely work 60-to-70-hour weeks under federal hours rules but currently receive straight-time pay for every hour. They would gain a legal right to time-and-a-half after 40 hours. Owner-operators who set their own hours would not benefit; the exemption applies to drivers employed by a carrier.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Salaried and hourly truck drivers at motor carriers

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the motor carrier exemption in Section 13(b)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, which since 1938 has let trucking companies pay their drivers straight time no matter how many hours they work.
Would give covered drivers a legal right to overtime pay at 1.5 times their regular rate after 40 hours in a workweek, the same standard most American workers already have.

analysis.who_pays: Motor carriers — the trucking companies — would bear new overtime payroll costs for their drivers. Some of that cost would likely be passed through to shippers as higher freight rates, and eventually to consumer prices. Drivers themselves would not pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Trucking companies, then shippers and consumers

drawbacks.text: Motor carriers would face higher labor costs, which in a thin-margin freight market would likely flow into higher shipping prices for businesses and consumers.

Drivers' total weekly hours are already capped by federal safety rules, so the gain is limited to weeks where employers schedule more than 40 hours; where hours are capped below that, overtime pay cannot accrue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and goes to a large, long-hours workforce that currently has no overtime right at all; the cost is higher payroll expense for carriers, some of which would reach consumers through freight rates. On balance a worker-side gain, though it would raise shipping costs somewhat and would not help owner-operators who work for themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew introduced the bill on November 9, 2023, joined by Rep. Mark Takano as an original cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which has jurisdiction over federal wage law.
No hearing, markup, or vote followed: the action history shows nothing after the committee referral for the rest of the 118th Congress.
The bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 2025, so the motor carrier overtime exemption remains in force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking companies came out ahead: they keep paying straight time for unlimited driver hours under the exemption the bill would have removed. Truck drivers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trucking companies that pay no overtime

for.name: Jefferson Van Drew
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Mark Takano
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), ranking member of the House Education and the Workforce subcommittee on workforce protections
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 2 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (including the original cosponsor).

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: American Trucking Associations and carrier industry groups
against.what_they_did: Have opposed removing the motor carrier overtime exemption, arguing drivers are well compensated and that federal hours-of-service rules already limit their hours.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored it and Democrats joined — 2 of 216 House Democrats and 1 of 224 House Republicans cosponsored — but with only 3 cosponsors and no vote ever held, the parties' full positions were never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the 1938 exemption that lets carriers pay drivers straight time for every hour worked, forcing overtime pay after 40 hours. Carriers' interest in keeping the exemption runs directly against drivers' interest in overtime wages.
Higher carrier labor costs would likely be passed through as higher freight rates. Like consumers, these businesses would absorb some of the cost the bill shifts to carriers.
